answer.summary: Choose a workplace where you can recruit and help people build their careers, where you can learn valuable skills, and where the engineering partnership and working alignment are strong. Don’t make top-brand status or speculative financial upside the deciding factors.

sections.heading: Choose a place where you can do right by your team
sections.content: For managers, Yehoshua advises going somewhere you can recruit. A useful bar is whether hiring people there will make their careers: will it be a good place for them to learn and grow? She says you should be able to earnestly tell candidates they can build their careers there.

sections.heading: Prioritize learning over prestige or predicted returns
sections.content: You don’t have to work at a top-brand company; there are many good companies and career paths. Focus on where you’ll learn. Companies can fail or stop growing, but skills endure. Yehoshua says financial success is especially hard to predict because markets and world events can change, and warns that taking a job simply because it pays a lot can be dangerous.

sections.heading: Check the partnership and alignment
sections.content: Before joining, assess whether you have a good engineering partner who can help get ideas built. Also make sure you agree on roles and responsibilities, where you’ll divide work, and where you need to stay aligned; conflicting direction from leaders can cause problems.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately attributes Yehoshua’s advice: choose a role where recruits can learn and advance their careers, prioritize durable learning and skills over brand prestige or uncertain financial returns, and assess engineering partnership and alignment. These claims are supported by the cited context, and both expected points are covered.
